publication_scope.blurb: Louis Le Blanc de Beaulieu - Sedan Theological Theses, newly rendered from the 1675 London Latin. Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-LX), and on the necessity of grace for moral good in fallen man (Pars Prior I-LIII; Pars Posterior, the Protestant doctrine, I-XXXII). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. It is a public-domain Latin Reformed retrieval on the same Fathers-site pipeline. The 1675 Pitt folio is Public Domain Mark 1.0. Do not treat the site as ante-Nicene only.

source_text: THESIS I. LEGIS Moralis & naturalis praecepta, juxta communem Protestantium Doctrinam, duobus modis observari possunt. Primum absolute, quoad operis materiam, sive quoad effectionem operis ipsius in se considerati. Deinde eo modo qui necessarius est, ut actio vere & in oculis Dei bona & honesta sit. Legem quoad operis materiam servare, est facere quod lex in genere praecipit, aut abstinere ab eo quod prohibet; Ut egenti subvenire, parentes honorare, ab homicidio, furto & adulterio abstinere, non habita ratione principii a quo fluit, aut finis ad quem tale opus refertur. Sed ut actio vere bona & honesta sit, requiritur praeterea ut ex debito principio fiat, & in finem quem Deus exigit referatur. Quae circumstantiae si desint, actio coram Deo vitiosa censetur, & peccati naturam induit.
english: Thesis I. According to the common doctrine of the Protestants, the precepts of the moral and natural law can be kept in two ways. The first is absolute: as to the matter of the work, that is, as to doing the work considered in itself. The second is the way required if an action is to be truly good and upright in God's sight.

To keep the law as to the matter of the work is to do what the law commands in general, or to abstain from what it forbids: to help the needy, honour one's parents, refrain from murder, theft and adultery, without regard to the principle the work flows from or the end it is referred to. For an action to be truly good and upright, it must in addition be done from a proper principle and be referred to the end God requires. If these circumstances are missing, the action is judged vicious before God and takes on the nature of sin.

source_text: II. Primo igitur apud Protestantes quaeritur an homo per peccatum corruptus, sine Dei gratia, & propriis liberi sui arbitrii viribus, possit legis moralis praecepta, saltem quoad operis materiam, implere? Ad quod communi consensu Respondent, quaedam esse legis moralis praecepta quae, nequidem secundum operis materiam, sive ut Schola Romana loquitur substantiam, ab homine lapso sine gratia servari possunt. Quale est praeceptum de non concupiscendo, & de Deo totis viribus & supra omnia diligendo.
english: Thesis II. The first question the Protestants ask, then, is whether man, corrupted by sin, can by the powers of his own free choice and without God's grace fulfil the precepts of the moral law, at least as to the matter of the work.

They answer with one accord that some precepts of the moral law cannot be kept by fallen man without grace, not even as to the matter of the work, or, in the Roman School's language, its substance. Such are the precept not to covet, and the precept to love God with all one's strength and above all things.

source_text: III. Nec minus in eo consentiunt, sine gratia Christi salutifera posse quaedam legis praecepta ab homine corrupto, saltem absolute & quoad operis materiam, servari. Id videre est apud Amesium in Bellarmino enervato. Concedimus etiam, inquit, posse hominem sine fide, cum auxilio speciali & etiam sine illo, bonum aliquod morale perficere, si perficere accipiatur pro effectione ipsius operis in se considerati, sine respectu principii a quo fluit, & finis ad quem referri debet, lib. 4. de libero Arbitrio capite tertio. Quibus consona sunt quae tradit Melanchton in Apologia confessionis Augustanae. Potest, inquit, humana voluntas aliquo modo efficere justitiam civilem, seu justitiam operum. Potest loqui de Deo, exhibere Deo certum cultum opere externo, obedire Magistratibus, parentibus in externo opere eligendo. Potest continere manus a caede, ab adulterio, a furto.
english: Thesis III. They agree no less that corrupt man can keep certain precepts of the law without the saving grace of Christ, at least absolutely and as to the matter of the work. This can be seen in Ames's Bellarmine Disarmed: 'We also grant that a man without faith, with special help and even without it, can perform some moral good, if "perform" is taken to mean doing the work considered in itself, without regard to the principle it flows from and the end to which it ought to be referred' (book 4, On free choice, chapter 3).

What Melanchthon teaches in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession agrees with this: 'The human will can in some measure achieve civil righteousness, or the righteousness of works. It can speak of God, offer God a certain worship by outward work, and obey magistrates and parents in choosing an outward work. It can keep its hands from murder, adultery and theft.'

source_text: IV. Neque ab his abludit quod docet Alexander Morus, bona moralia absolute spectata ab homine in statu peccati perfici posse. Potest enim, inquit, quivis caste sobrieque vivere quoad actus externos, manus a furto & homicidio abstinere, locomotivam regere, coetibus Ecclesiae interesse, Evangelium audire libenter, non instar surdae aspidis aures obturare: quae omnia honesta sunt & civilia, Deoque minus ingrata quando utcunque usurpantur, quam ubi profana contemptione omittuntur. De Victoria gratiae disputatione secunda, Thesi 41.
english: Thesis IV. Nor is this far from what Alexander Morus teaches: that moral goods, taken absolutely, can be performed by man in the state of sin. 'Anyone can,' he says, 'live chastely and soberly as far as outward acts go, keep his hands from theft and murder, govern his power of movement, attend the gatherings of the Church, and hear the Gospel gladly instead of stopping his ears like the deaf adder.

All these things are upright and civil, and God finds them less displeasing when they are practised in whatever way than when they are left undone out of profane contempt' (On the Victory of Grace, second disputation, thesis 41).

source_text: V. Et certe ipsa experientia planum est hominem etiam Ethnicum & nulla salutari Dei cognitione imbutum, posse depositum & mutuum reddere, cognatos colere, parentes honorare, Eleemosynam pauperibus largiri, temperanter & sobrie vivere, & plura ejusmodi: & sic multa facere apud homines, quos interiora latent, speciosa & laudabilia: & ex quibus exurgit justitia quaedam & honestas civilis: qualis fuit in Socrate, Epaminonda, Phocione, Scipione, Catone, & pluribus apud Gentiles laudatis viris, quorum exempla plerisque Christianis pudorem suffundere debent.
english: Thesis V. Experience itself makes it plain that a man, even a pagan with no saving knowledge of God, can repay a deposit or a loan, care for his relatives, honour his parents, give alms to the poor, live temperately and soberly, and do many other such things.

In this way he can do many things that look fine and praiseworthy before men, who cannot see what lies within, and from them arises a kind of righteousness and civil uprightness. Such was found in Socrates, Epaminondas, Phocion, Scipio, Cato and many other men praised among the Gentiles, whose examples ought to make most Christians blush.

source_text: VI. Quamvis autem, ex Protestantium sensu, ad ejusmodi civilem justitiam atque honestatem gratia Christi necessaria non sit; multi tamen eorum observant illam speciali cuidam Dei auxilio esse tribuendam. Homines enim prorsus sibi relictos, nequidem ejusmodi civilem justitiam assequi posse, & qui apud Ethnicos virtutis nomine laudantur, non sine Deo singulari modo auxiliante, & nativam eorum corruptionem coercente, laudabiles ullas actiones egisse: Absque hoc enim futurum fuisse, ut non minus quam alii plurimi, in execranda quaeque facinora ruerent.
english: Thesis VI. Although in the Protestants' view the grace of Christ is not needed for civil righteousness and uprightness of this kind, many of them point out that it is to be ascribed to a special help of God.

Men left wholly to themselves, they say, could not attain even this civil righteousness, and those praised among the pagans for virtue did no praiseworthy actions without God helping them in a singular way and restraining their native corruption. Without this they would have rushed, no less than very many others, into every abominable crime.

source_text: VII. Quae sententia est Mosis Amyraldi disputatione de Libero arbitrio. Mea sententia, inquit, si Deus omnes homines nativae suae corruptioni permitteret, omnemque Providentiae suae efficacitatem sustineret, tum quae versatur in temperamento corporis moderando, tum quae sese exerit in cujusque hominis animo vel regendo, vel coercendo, vel ad virtutis qualecunque studium incitando, nemo esset qui injustitia, libidine, truculentia, avaritia, & omni vitiorum foeditate Nerones, & Caligulas, & Sardanapalos, & quosvis alios e numero desperatissimorum, non aequaret, aut superaret, pag. 173.
english: Thesis VII. This is the view of Moïse Amyraut in his disputation On free choice. 'In my opinion,' he says, 'if God abandoned all men to their native corruption and withheld all the efficacy of his providence, both the providence at work in moderating the temperament of the body and the providence that exerts itself in each man's mind, ruling or restraining it or spurring it to some kind of pursuit of virtue, there would be no one who would not equal or surpass the Neros, Caligulas and Sardanapaluses, or any others among the most desperate, in injustice, lust, cruelty, avarice and every foulness of vice' (page 173).

source_text: VIII. Quibus consentanea sunt quae docet Alexander Morus jam citata Disputatione. Porro, inquit, libertas illa, qua leges condunt, Rempublicam temperant, in commune consulunt, victorias reportant, & virtutibus variis praelucent, etiam ii qui versantur in statu peccati, non ita locum habet in iis, quasi ex ipsius naturae incunabulis existeret. A Deo enim est luminum Patre, a quo donum omne bonum descendit, quod illi ipsi agnoverunt, quum neminem virum insignem oriri absque divino afflatu scribunt: & ratio ipsa persuadebat: cur enim Heroum filii tam degeneres, cur eodem partu editi tam dissimiles occurrerent? cur educatione optima imbuti immanes belluae fierent? thesi quadragesima sexta. Quibus thesi sequenti subjicit, Nempe Dei provida manus in ipso exortu probae indolis quaedam veluti semina spargit, ac deinde culturae opportunitates objicit, quae tamen parum prodessent, nisi hominum nequitiae Deus spiritus sui habenis moderaretur: nam cum velit humanam societatem ordine legitimo contineri, omnium pariter ferocire proterviam non sinit, sed alios metu poenae compescit, alios amore praemii accendit: alioqui summa rerum esset confusio, si quam proni sunt omnes ad mala omne genus, tam in ea prorumperent.
english: Thesis VIII. What Alexander Morus teaches in the disputation already cited agrees with this. 'Further,' he says, 'the liberty by which men make laws, govern the state, take counsel for the common good, win victories and shine in various virtues, even those who live in the state of sin, is not present in them as if it arose from the very cradle of nature. It comes from God, the Father of lights, from whom every good gift comes down. They acknowledged this themselves when they wrote that no distinguished man arises without divine inspiration, and reason itself convinced them. Otherwise why would the sons of heroes so degenerate, why would twins born together turn out so unlike, and why would men trained in the best education become savage beasts?' (thesis 46).

In the next thesis he adds: 'God's provident hand scatters, as it were, certain seeds of a good disposition at a man's very birth, and then puts opportunities for cultivating them in his way. These would do little good, though, unless God curbed men's wickedness with the reins of his Spirit. Since he wills that human society be held together in lawful order, he does not let everyone's insolence run wild alike, but restrains some by fear of punishment and kindles others by love of reward. Otherwise everything would be in utter confusion, if men broke out into evils of every kind as far as they are all inclined to them.'

source_text: IX. Itaque ex horum Doctorum sententia si natura hominis in se consideretur, omnes homines pares nascuntur, nec alter altero melior aut pejor est: quod vero discrimen inter eos hac in parte cernitur, tribuendum est arcanae Dei dispensationi, per quam hominum affectus, non intus purgantur quidem, sed coercentur ne ferventius ebulliant. Quamvis enim lateat in singulorum pectoribus quaedam veluti Lerna malorum omne genus, tamen alios Deus indulgere vitiis, & quibusdam veluti furiis agitari patitur: alios pudore, legum reverentia, existimationis bonae, ac immortalis famae amore tangit & in officio quadantenus continet: ut quod omnes Imperatores non fuerunt Caligulae, aut caeteri homines Timoni similes, non id naturae quae mater aliis, aliis fuerit noverca imputemus, sed Deum agnoscamus alios permittentem suae libidini, alios variis modis fraenantem atque reprimentem.
english: Thesis IX. So, in the opinion of these divines, if man's nature is considered in itself, all men are born equal, and none is better or worse than another. Whatever difference appears between them in this respect is to be ascribed to God's secret dispensation, by which men's passions are not cleansed within but are held in check so that they do not boil over more violently.

For although a Lerna of every kind of evil lies hidden in each person's breast, God lets some indulge their vices and be driven as if by furies. Others he moves by shame, respect for the laws, and the love of a good name and of undying fame, and keeps them to some extent within their duty. So the fact that not all emperors were Caligulas, nor all other men like Timon, is not something we should credit to nature, as if she were a mother to some and a stepmother to others. We should recognise God, who leaves some to their lust and curbs and holds back others in various ways.

source_text: X. Ex Protestantium igitur sententia, ab homine in statu peccati, & sine gratia Christi multa fieri possunt civiliter bona & honesta, quae singulari cuidam efficacitati divinae providentiae tribui merentur. Et ista quidem talia sunt, ut minus malos reddant eos in quibus reperiuntur, & apud homines laude digna censeri possint. Imo quae sunt ejusmodi Deus interdum aliquo temporali praemio remuneratur. Sic nempe, inquit Alexander Morus, quam sibi placeant vere bona significat, quum illam tenuem bonitatis umbram indonatam abire non patitur. Deinde ad exemplum ita se comparat, ut caeteri ad meliorem frugem invitentur. Ac insuper quemadmodum, si omnes pii florerent in hoc seculo, vix homines judicium futurum expectarent: ita quum aliquando certe vident iis esse melius qui aliqua pietatis cura tanguntur, de providentia numinis admonentur. Denique pro ratione bonitatis quae fulget in opere, Deus praemium temporale admetitur: & curta fluxaque bona rependit externae virtuti, qui cursui spirituali coeleste ac aeternum Regnum constituit. Jam allegata Disputatione thesi 45.
english: Thesis X. In the Protestants' view, then, many things that are civilly good and upright can be done by man in the state of sin and without the grace of Christ, and they deserve to be ascribed to a singular efficacy of divine providence. Such acts make those in whom they are found less bad, and among men they can be judged praiseworthy. Indeed, God sometimes rewards things of this kind with some temporal reward.

'In this way,' says Alexander Morus, 'he shows how much truly good things please him, since he does not let even that faint shadow of goodness go unrewarded. Then he acts so as to make it an example, inviting the rest to do better.

Moreover, if all the godly prospered in this world, men would hardly look for the judgement to come. So when they sometimes see plainly that things go better for those who have some concern for godliness, they are reminded of the providence of God. Finally, God measures out a temporal reward in proportion to the goodness that shines in the work. He repays outward virtue with short-lived and passing goods, he who has appointed a heavenly and eternal kingdom for the spiritual course' (the disputation already cited, thesis 45).

source_text: XI. Verum communi consensu statuunt Protestantes nullum bonum morale in hoc statu naturae corruptae, sine gratia Christi, ab homine sic perfici posse, ut actio coram Deo revera bona & justa habeatur, neque peccatis debeat accenseri. Ac proinde quaecunque ab hominibus sine Christi gratia fiunt, ut ut speciem virtutis habeant, & externam aliquam bonitatem atque honestatem, peccati rationem in judicio Dei non effugere; adeoque pulcherrima & illustrissima heroum facinora, splendida esse peccata, larvas & simulachra virtutum: ut cum Augustino loquitur saepe jam dictus Morus thesi 42. Bellarminus, inquit, per moralia opera, quae Deo jucunda sunt & qualia Deus postulat, intellexit: quo sensu plane nihil hominem posse, atque adeo pulcherrima ipsius & illustrissima facinora splendida, esse peccata, larvas & simulachra virtutum Augustino facile credimus. Quibus conforme est quod apud Davidem Paraeum legitur, Dicimus, inquit, morales non renatorum virtutes qualescunque, sine fide cum immunditia cordis factas, ut maxime coram mundo sint honestae, justae, laude & praemiis dignae: tamen coram Deo esse peccata, non quidem suo genere, sed per accidens. In lib. 5. Bellar. de gratia & libero Arbitrio, cap. 4. Dicit autem tales virtutes esse peccata per accidens, quoniam licet res sint ex suo genere bonae, in quibusdam tamen essentialibus deficiunt: nempe quia nec ex debito principio oriuntur, nec referuntur in legitimum finem.
english: Thesis XI. The Protestants, however, hold with one accord that in this state of corrupted nature no moral good can be performed by man without the grace of Christ in such a way that the act is held truly good and just before God and is not to be counted among sins. So whatever men do without the grace of Christ, however much it has the look of virtue and some outward goodness and uprightness, does not escape the character of sin in God's judgement. Thus the finest and most glorious deeds of heroes are splendid sins, masks and likenesses of virtues, as Morus, often cited already, puts it with Augustine in thesis 42.

'By moral works,' he says, 'Bellarmine meant works that please God and such as God requires. In that sense we readily believe Augustine that man can do nothing at all, and that even his finest and most glorious deeds are splendid sins, masks and likenesses of virtues.' What we read in David Pareus agrees with this: 'We say that the moral virtues of the unregenerate, of whatever kind, done without faith and with an unclean heart, however upright, just and worthy of praise and reward they may be before the world, are nonetheless sins before God, not in their kind but by accident' (on Bellarmine, On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 4).

He calls such virtues sins by accident because, though they are good things in their kind, they fall short in certain essentials. They do not arise from the proper principle, and they are not referred to the lawful end.

source_text: XII. Quod enim actiones hominis peccatoris sine Christi gratia factae, quamvis ex suo genere, & secundum operis materiam bonae sint, revera tamen, secundum Protestantium doctrinam, rationem peccati habeant, causa est, quia neque ex Dei amore procedunt, neque ad Dei gloriam diriguntur. Utrumque enim ad opus quodlibet vere bonum, & Dei judicio tale, plane necessarium putant: neutrum vero in homine Lapso sine gratia Christi salutifera locum habere posse existimant.
english: Thesis XII. The reason why, on Protestant doctrine, the acts of a sinner done without the grace of Christ really have the character of sin, though they are good in their kind and as to the matter of the work, is that they neither proceed from the love of God nor are directed to his glory.

The Protestants hold that both of these are plainly necessary for any work that is truly good and good in God's judgement, and they consider that neither can be found in fallen man without the saving grace of Christ.

source_text: XIII. Et quidem quod nullum opus, secundum naturae legem, vere bonum esse possit, nisi fluat ex Dei amore, inde probant, quod illa naturae lex ab homine exigit, ut Deum creatorem suum, a cujus bonitate habet quicquid est, & potest, totis viribus & supra omnia diligat. Qui autem ex solo creaturarum amore, non vero ex amore Dei ad agendum movetur, in eo testatur se Deum supra creaturas omnes non diligere, sed creaturae amorem amori divino praeferre, ac proinde vitiose agit.
english: Thesis XIII. That no work can be truly good by the law of nature unless it flows from the love of God, they prove from the fact that this law of nature requires man to love God his creator, from whose goodness he has all that he is and all that he can do, with all his strength and above all things.

Whoever is moved to act by love of creatures alone, and not by love of God, shows by this that he does not love God above all creatures. He prefers love of the creature to love of God, and so he acts viciously.

source_text: XIV. Caeterum frustra hic distinguunt nonnulli quendam amorem Dei virtualem atque implicitum, ab amore Dei formali atque explicito: quasi aliquis Deum formaliter non diligens, imo Deum ignorans, censeri tamen posset illum implicite amare, cum diligit actiones quasdam a Deo praeceptas, quae hoc ipso Deo placere censendae sunt. Nam qui Deum ignorat, aut non operatur ex Dei amore, vel actuali vel habituali, proculdubio ex sui amore operatur, ac seipsum supra omnia diligit; nec actionem honestam diligit, nisi ut ea gaudeat, atque sibi placeat. Omnis vero sui amor qui divino non subordinatur, vitiosus & peccaminosus est. In amore autem aliquo vitioso laudabilem quendam Dei amorem implicitum esse, prorsus est contra rationem.
english: Thesis XIV. It is useless for some to distinguish here between a virtual, implicit love of God and a formal, explicit one, as though someone who does not formally love God, and is even ignorant of him, could still be reckoned to love him implicitly when he loves certain actions God has commanded, actions that must for that very reason be reckoned pleasing to God.

For whoever does not know God, or does not act from love of God, whether actual or habitual, undoubtedly acts from love of himself and loves himself above all things. He loves an upright action only so that he may take joy in it and be pleased with himself. Every love of self not subordinated to the love of God is vicious and sinful, and it is wholly unreasonable to find a praiseworthy implicit love of God inside a vicious love.

source_text: XV. Similiter eadem naturae lex postulat, ut creatura rationalis omnes suas actiones ad Dei gloriam dirigat: quandoquidem Dei gloria est naturalis rerum omnium finis: quoniam universa propter semetipsum operatus est Dominus. Et ex ipso, & per ipsum, & in ipsum sunt omnia. Adeoque ad naturae legem pertinet Pauli praeceptum, Omnia in Dei gloriam facite. Ac proinde nulla actio quam agens ad Dei gloriam non refert, revera bona & justa esse potest: cum actionum bonitas ex legitimo fine praecipue metienda sit. Prov. 16. 4. Rom. 11. 36. 1 Cor. 10. 31.
english: Thesis XV. In the same way the law of nature requires the rational creature to direct all its actions to the glory of God. God's glory is the natural end of all things, for 'the Lord has made all things for himself', and 'of him, through him and to him are all things'. Paul's precept, 'Do all to the glory of God', therefore belongs to the law of nature.

So no act that the agent does not refer to the glory of God can be truly good and just, since the goodness of actions is to be measured chiefly by their lawful end (Proverbs 16:4; Romans 11:36; 1 Corinthians 10:31).

source_text: XVI. Neque est quod quis dicat ad Dei gloriam quodammodo referri actiones quae fiunt ob finem aliquem non malum, etiamsi agens de eo non cogitet. Exempli causa, quum aliquis verum Deum non cognoscens pecuniam egenti largitur, ut ei subveniat, ejusmodi actionem ad Dei gloriam spectare: quoniam omnis quae est in rebus creatis bonitas ad Deum per se spectat atque refertur. Nec enim ut actio in Dei gloriam fieri censenda sit, sufficit ut finis ejus res sit naturaliter bona, & proinde quae ex sua natura ad Deum referri queat. Alioqui qui laborat non alium ob finem, quam ut opes acquirat, posset dici in Dei gloriam laborare, siquidem opes per se res bona, non mala sunt. Et tamen labor ejusmodi proculdubio labor improbus est, & ad vitium non ad virtutem spectat.
english: Thesis XVI. Nor can anyone say that acts done for some end that is not bad are in some way referred to God's glory even if the agent does not think of it. Suppose, for example, that someone who does not know the true God gives money to a person in need in order to help him. It would be argued that such an act looks to God's glory, since all the goodness in created things looks to God of itself and is referred to him.

But for an act to be counted as done for God's glory, it is not enough that its end is something naturally good, which by its nature could be referred to God. Otherwise a man who works for no other end than to get rich could be said to work for God's glory, since wealth is in itself a good thing and not a bad one. Yet such work is undoubtedly wicked, and tends toward vice, not virtue.

source_text: XVII. Jam vero Deum supra omnia diligere, & actiones suas ad ejus gloriam referre, res est quae ad Dei spiritualem cultum & pietatem maxime pertinet. Et ex consequenti certum esse debet ad hoc omnino necessariam esse salutiferam Jesu Christi gratiam, sine qua, fatente tota Schola Romana, nihil valet prorsus liberum hominis lapsi arbitrium ad spirituale bonum volendum & perficiendum. Ex quibus omnibus merito concludunt Protestantes hominem Christi gratia destitutum, & in simplici lapsae naturae statu, nihil facere posse quod boni moralis veram rationem obtineat, & apud Deum vere justum atque honestum habeatur: Quandoquidem homines sibi prorsus relicti, & a vero fine in agendo aberrant, & ex malo principio, amore scilicet proprio, operantur.
english: Thesis XVII. To love God above all things and to refer one's actions to his glory belongs above all to the spiritual worship of God and to godliness. It follows that the saving grace of Jesus Christ must certainly be wholly necessary for it, since without that grace, as the whole Roman School admits, the free choice of fallen man can do nothing at all toward willing and doing spiritual good.

From all this the Protestants rightly conclude that a man without the grace of Christ, in the bare state of fallen nature, can do nothing that has the true character of moral good and is held truly just and upright before God. Men left wholly to themselves both miss the true end in what they do and act from a bad principle, namely love of self.

source_text: XVIII. His consentanea sunt quae leguntur apud Josuam Placeum tractatu de Libero hominis arbitrio. Ubi postquam docuit Adamum amisisse libertatem absolutam non peccandi, & in ejus locum successisse servitutem peccati, sitam in depravatione atque obliquitate facultatum moralium, praesertim voluntatis; eam vero depravationem consistere in aversione a vero fine ultimo, & conversione ad finem ultimum falso apparentem: Ex quo sequitur, cum quicquid appetitur, sit aut finis ultimus aut medium ad illum, nihil sani reliquum esse factum in facultatibus nostris moralibus, & quamdiu sic affecti sumus fieri non posse quin peccemus, hujus rei rationem subjungit his verbis. Nam seu appetamus finem ultimum, seu media, aberramus semper a vero scopo, quantumcunque virtutum splendore lucere videatur homo irregenitus, quia quicquid appetit, quicquid loquitur & agit, in scopum ultimum collineat, qui falso illi apparet scopus, cum plurimum absit a vero scopo, & eo ipso peccat, nec potest non peccare, quamdiu male judicat de scopo. pag. 199.
english: Thesis XVIII. With these agree what we read in Josué de la Place's treatise On man's free choice. He first teaches that Adam lost the absolute liberty of not sinning, and that the bondage of sin took its place. That bondage lies in the depravity and crookedness of the moral faculties, especially the will, and the depravity consists in turning away from the true last end and turning toward a last end that only appears to be one.

It follows, since whatever is desired is either the last end or a means to it, that nothing sound is left in our moral faculties, and that as long as we are in this condition we cannot help sinning. He then gives the reason in these words: 'Whether we seek the last end or the means, we always miss the true mark, however brightly the unregenerate man may seem to shine with virtues. For whatever he desires, says or does, he aims at a last goal that falsely appears to him to be the goal, though it is very far from the true one. By that very fact he sins, and he cannot help sinning as long as he judges wrongly about the goal' (page 199).

source_text: XIX. Similiter Alexander Morus observat peccatorem gratia Dei carentem variis modis deficere in quibuslibet operibus, quantumvis alioquin eximia videantur, quo fit ut apud Deum, qui secundum rei veritatem judicat, revera non bona sed mala censeantur, quoniam bonum est ex integra causa, malum ex defectu vel unius circumstantiae. Quippe quatuor defectus in operibus ejusmodi notat, respectu principii, subjecti, modi, & finis. Eorum enim principium non est Spiritus, sed caro, id est, affectus carnalis, fructus autem carnis placere Deo nequeunt. Subjectum est homo destitutus gratia illa per quam εὐαρέστως λατρεύομεν τῷ Θεῷ, id est, cultum Deo placentem exhibemus. Modus ex aliqua generositate, non ex fide petitur, sine qua nemo Deo placet. Ac demum finis plane desideratur, salus proximi, gloria Dei. In victoria Gratiae Disput. 2. thesi 43.
english: Thesis XIX. Alexander Morus likewise observes that a sinner who lacks God's grace falls short in many ways in all his works, however excellent they may otherwise seem. So before God, who judges by the truth of the matter, they are really counted not good but bad, since good comes from a cause that is whole, and evil from the lack of even one circumstance.

He notes four defects in works of this kind, in their principle, their subject, their manner and their end. Their principle is not the Spirit but the flesh, that is, carnal affection, and the fruits of the flesh cannot please God. Their subject is a man without the grace by which 'we serve God acceptably', that is, offer God a worship that pleases him. Their manner is drawn from some generosity of spirit, not from faith, and without faith no one pleases God. Finally their end, the salvation of one's neighbour and the glory of God, is wholly missing (On the Victory of Grace, disputation 2, thesis 43).

source_text: XX. Verum est quidem etiam piorum & justorum opera per gratiam Dei facta suos quoque naevos & defectus habere; sed hi defectus sunt tantum accidentales, qui boni operis essentiam non tollunt. Qui vero vitiant opera eorum qui sunt Christi gratia destituti, sunt defectus essentiales, cum quibus salva manere non potest ipsa boni operis natura atque essentia. Siquidem operis bonitas praecipue pendet a fine in quem tendit, & a principio unde oritur. Sed hominis qui est gratiae Christi expers, opera omnia, ut supra ostendimus, & a vero fine aberrant, qui est Dei gloria; & a malo principio, cupiditate, scilicet, terrena originem ducunt: per quae opus alioqui ex suo genere bonum, omnino vitiatur. Piorum vero & justorum opera procedunt a Dei amore, & ad ejus gloriam tendunt, ac in eo solum deficiunt, quod nec in iis tam pure Dei gloria quaeritur, nec Dei amor unde fluunt tantum fervorem habet, quam par esset. Adeoque piorum opera imperfecte quidem sed vere bona sunt; eorum vero qui gratia Christi carent opera quaevis, ut ut in oculis hominum luceant, coram Deo revera mala sunt, nec boni operis naturam retinent: licet alia sint aliis minus mala.
english: Thesis XX. It is true that even the works of the godly and righteous, done through God's grace, have their own blemishes and defects. But those defects are only accidental and do not take away the essence of a good work. The defects that spoil the works of those without the grace of Christ are essential ones, and the very nature and essence of a good work cannot survive them. A work's goodness depends chiefly on the end it tends to and the principle it springs from.

Yet all the works of a man without the grace of Christ, as shown above, miss the true end, which is God's glory, and take their origin from a bad principle, earthly desire. That ruins a work that would otherwise be good in its kind. The works of the godly and righteous proceed from love of God and tend to his glory. Their only shortfall is that God's glory is not sought in them as purely as it should be, and the love of God they flow from is not as fervent as it ought to be.

So the works of the godly are good, imperfectly but truly. Whatever works are done by those who lack the grace of Christ, however brightly they shine in men's eyes, are really bad before God and do not keep the nature of a good work, though some are less bad than others.

source_text: XXI. Istud observat Alexander Morus Disputatione saepius jam citata thesi quadragesima quarta. Opera infidelium, inquit, bona non sunt, sed alia sunt aliis minus mala. Opera vero fidelium tametsi respersa maculis & varie mutila & imperfecte bona, bona tamen, vere bona sunt — languide ingrediuntur, sed in via salutis; ac debili motu, sed in scopum jaculantur: alii citato cursu feruntur, sed extra viam, & arcum strenue tendunt, sed non in verum scopum destinant.
english: Thesis XXI. Alexander Morus notes this in the disputation already cited so often, thesis 44. 'The works of unbelievers,' he says, 'are not good; some are only less bad than others. The works of the faithful, though stained with spots, maimed in various ways and imperfectly good, are still good, truly good.

They go forward feebly, but on the way of salvation; they throw with weak motion, but at the mark. The others race along at speed, but off the road; they draw the bow hard, but do not aim at the true mark.'

source_text: XXII. Caeterum ex dictis facile colligitur, secundum Protestantes, nullum opus esse vere bonum in genere morum, quod non etiam ad salutem aeternam ordinetur, & partem faciat cultus & pietatis erga Deum, quandoquidem nihil boni operis nomine dignantur quod non in gloriam Dei collineet, & ex dilectione illius oriatur. Proinde apud eos locum non habet illa distinctio bonorum operum quae in Schola Romana obtinet, ut sint quaedam duntaxat naturaliter & moraliter bona, sed vere bona tamen, etiam in Dei oculis, quanquam ad salutem aeternam non prosint: alia vero quae prosint ad salutem, & supernaturalem bonitatem habeant. Etenim, juxta ipsos, omnia opera quae vere bona sunt, a supernaturali principio ortum habent, a gratia Christi, videlicet, & etiam ad vitam aeternam aliquid conferunt. Quod si quandoque operibus eorum qui sunt extra Christi gratiam moralem, aliquam bonitatem tribuunt, eo nomine designant bonitatem quandam solum externam & civilem, & quae non reddit opus Deo gratum & placens, nec obstat quominus reipsa peccatum sit, & dici mereatur.
english: Thesis XXII. From what has been said it is easy to gather that, on the Protestant view, no work is truly good in the moral order unless it is also ordered to eternal salvation and forms part of worship and godliness toward God. For they count nothing worthy of the name of a good work unless it aims at God's glory and springs from love of him.

So the distinction among good works that holds in the Roman School has no place with them: that some works are merely naturally and morally good, yet still truly good even in God's sight, though they do nothing toward eternal salvation, while others help toward salvation and have a supernatural goodness. On their view all truly good works originate in a supernatural principle, namely the grace of Christ, and also contribute something toward eternal life.

If they sometimes ascribe a moral goodness to the works of those outside the grace of Christ, they mean by it a goodness that is only outward and civil. It does not make the work acceptable and pleasing to God, and it does not stop it from really being a sin and deserving the name.

source_text: XXIII. Caeterum in hac quaestione, gratiae Christi nomine non dignantur auxilia illa ordinis naturalis quae Deus non denegat infidelibus ipsis in infidelitate sua permanentibus: Sed gratiam Christi vocant eam duntaxat quae incipit a fide, & ea non qualicunque, verum Christiana & divinitus infusa, quaeque iners & mortua non sit, sed quae per dilectionem operari incipiat.
english: Thesis XXIII. In this question, however, they do not give the name 'grace of Christ' to the helps of the natural order that God does not refuse even to unbelievers who remain in their unbelief.

They call grace of Christ only the grace that begins with faith, and not with faith of just any kind, but with Christian faith infused by God, which is not idle and dead but begins to work through love.

source_text: XXIV. Adeoque omnia infidelium opera, quantumvis speciosa, inter peccata connumerant. Ac pro infidelibus habent, non solum eos qui prorsus verum Deum ignorant, verum etiam omnes illos qui vera in Christum fide destituuntur, nec cognoscunt unum solum verum Deum, & quem misit Jesum Christum. Omnium qui tales sunt opera, quamlibet egregia & honesta videantur, non actus verae virtutis, sed peccata illius colore fucata esse existimant, ut ex jam dictis satis manifestum est. Quoniam sine fide Deo placere nihil potest, & peccatum est quicquid fit sine fide, non ea solum quae conscientiae fluctuanti opponitur, sed ea quoque quae conscientiam ex Dei verbo ut par est informat, & certam reddit, & etiam hominem justificare valet. Haec est doctrina Davidis Paraei. Dicimus, inquit, ad opus morale bonum, quod sit ad legem, cultum & beneplacitum Dei ordinatum, requiri non modo speciale auxilium singularis providentiae Dei, nec modo specialem gratiam singularis motionis divinae, sed etiam specialem gratiam fidei justificantis. In Bellarm. lib. 5. de Gratia & libero Arbitrio, capite 4.
english: Thesis XXIV. They therefore count all the works of unbelievers, however fine they look, among sins. And they reckon as unbelievers not only those wholly ignorant of the true God but all who lack true faith in Christ and do not know the one true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. They hold that the works of all such people, however excellent and upright they seem, are not acts of true virtue but sins painted in its colours, as is clear enough from what has already been said.

For without faith nothing can please God, and whatever is done without faith is sin. By faith here they mean not only the faith opposed to a wavering conscience, but the faith that shapes the conscience from God's word as it should, makes it certain, and is even able to justify a man.

This is David Pareus's teaching: 'We say that a morally good work, one ordered to God's law, worship and good pleasure, requires not only the special help of God's singular providence, and not only the special grace of a singular divine motion, but also the special grace of justifying faith' (on Bellarmine, On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 4).

source_text: XXV. Neque simpliciter asserunt Protestantes gratiam per quam fides ingeneratur, necessariam esse ad quodvis bonum opus, & neminem sine illa verum & Deo gratum obsequium legi naturali praestare; sed praeterea satis aperte docent, gratiam illam sine qua nemo bene operari potest, & vel unicum opus revera bonum efficere, esse ipsam gratiam regenerantem & justificantem. Id praesertim videre est apud Josuam Placeum, qui negat hominem posse non peccare sine gratia regenerationis. Haec enim sunt illius verba. Ad morales quod attinet actiones, quas, scilicet, lex aut praecipit aut prohibet, multiplicat quaestiones Bellarminus sine ulla necessitate. Nos ad hanc unam quicquid nobis est cum Pontificiis controversiae de Libero Arbitrio in statu peccati revocamus, Possit ne homo irregenitus non peccare sine gratia regenerationis? affirmant Pontificii, nos negamus. Tractatu de libero Arbitrio pag. 201. Quibus consonat quod apud Amesium legitur in Bellarmino enervato. Primo, inquit, nostri docent nihil boni spiritualis efficere hominem posse antequam sit regenitus: sed Bellarminus auxilium gratiae suadentis & assistentis tantum requirit. Secundo, nostri illud auxilium requirunt ad bonum spirituale, quod est proprium efficaciter vocatorum: sed Bellarminus auxilium generale intelligit, quod pro loco & tempore nemini deest. Lib. 4. de libero Arbitrio cap. 3. Ubi sub nomine boni spiritualis complectitur quicquid vere bonum est in genere morum: quoniam, ut supra ostendi, Protestantes in hoc genere nihil revera bonum existimant, quod non ex sincera Dei dilectione procedat, adeoque ad pietatem & spiritualem Dei cultum aliquo modo pertineat.
english: Thesis XXV. The Protestants do not merely say that the grace by which faith is produced is needed for every good work, and that no one can offer the natural law a true obedience pleasing to God without it. They also teach openly enough that the grace without which no one can act well, or do even one truly good work, is regenerating and justifying grace itself.

This can be seen especially in Josué de la Place, who denies that a man can avoid sinning without the grace of regeneration. His words are these: 'As for moral actions, those the law commands or forbids, Bellarmine multiplies questions needlessly. We bring our whole dispute with the Papists over free choice in the state of sin back to this one question: can an unregenerate man avoid sinning without the grace of regeneration? The Papists say yes; we say no' (treatise On free choice, page 201).

What we read in Ames's Bellarmine Disarmed agrees with this. 'First,' he says, 'our divines teach that man can do nothing of spiritual good before he is born again, whereas Bellarmine requires only the help of a grace that persuades and assists. Second, our divines require for spiritual good the help that is proper to those effectually called, whereas Bellarmine means a general help that is lacking to no one at the right place and time' (book 4, On free choice, chapter 3).

There Ames includes under 'spiritual good' everything truly good in the moral order. For, as I showed above, the Protestants count nothing in this order as truly good unless it proceeds from a sincere love of God and so belongs in some way to godliness and the spiritual worship of God.

source_text: XXVI. Quod vero ante justificationem, ex Protestantium sensu, nemo possit ullum opus vere bonum facere, inde patet quod censura sua notant Canonem illum synodi Tridentinae, qui est septimus sessionis sextae. Si quis dixerit opera omnia, quae ante justificationem fiunt, quacunque ratione facta sint, vere esse peccata, vel odium Dei mereri, aut quanto vehementius quis nititur se disponere ad gratiam, tanto eum gravis peccare, anathema sit. Ac praeterea frequenter laudant & probant quod dicit Augustinus, Bona opera sequi justificatum, non praecedere justificandum. Ut praesertim videre est apud Calvinum in Antidoto Synodi Tridentinae ad Canonem citatum. Et apud Kemnitium in examine ejusdem Synodi, ubi agit de praeparatione ad justificationem.
english: Thesis XXVI. That on the Protestant view no one can do any truly good work before justification is plain from their censure of the Council of Trent's canon 7 of the sixth session: 'If anyone says that all works done before justification, in whatever way they are done, are truly sins or deserve God's hatred, or that the harder anyone strives to dispose himself for grace, the more grievously he sins, let him be anathema.'

They also often praise and approve Augustine's saying: 'Good works follow the one who is justified; they do not go before the one who is to be justified.' This can be seen especially in Calvin's Antidote to the Council of Trent on that canon, and in Chemnitz's Examination of the same council, where he treats of preparation for justification.

source_text: XXVII. Hac autem in parte videtur doctrina Protestantium non carere difficultate. Et enim qui inter eos de rebus Theologicis accuratius Philosophantur, agnoscunt fidem, eamque vivam & actuosam, esse conditionem ad justificationem hominis praerequisitam. Jam vero credere in Deum est quoddam opus vere bonum, neque fides viva est sine aliqua Dei dilectione, quae ipsa quoque est quoddam bonum opus; adeoque opera quaedam quae justificationem praecedunt, sunt vere bona.
english: Thesis XXVII. On this point, however, Protestant doctrine does not seem free from difficulty. Those among them who reason most exactly about theological matters acknowledge that faith, and a living and active faith, is a prerequisite condition of a man's justification.
Yet believing in God is a truly good work, and living faith does not exist without some love of God, which is itself a good work too. So some works that precede justification are truly good.

source_text: XXVIII. Fatentur etiam resipiscentiam, sive poenitentiam esse conditionem sub qua remissio peccatorum, in qua hominis peccatoris justificatio consistit, offertur in Evangelio. Sic docet celeberrimus Maresius peccatorum remissionem resipiscentiae competere Conditionaliter, prout haec nobis sub resipiscentiae & fidei conditione offertur in Evangelio Disputatione de Resipiscentia & libertate Christiana, Thesi 32. Et similiter Amesius in Bellarmino Enervato libro quinto de fide justificante capite tertio, Concedit poenitentiam antecedere justificationem ut dispositionem ex ordine praerequisitam, sed non ut causam. Quod idem videre est apud Kemnitium ipsum loco modo citato. Jam autem in poenitentia & resipiscentia bona opera multa involvuntur, quale est vitae novae propositum, peccati detestatio, & quaedam etiam dilectio Dei, quae oritur ex spe veniae a Deo obtinendae. Ac proinde non pauca bona opera praecedunt justificationem. Quin idem Amesius loco jam allegato disertis verbis agnoscit Dei Dilectionem aliquam esse priorem remissione peccatorum, sive justificatione, ut dispositionem praerequisitam, licet dilectio nulla remissionem praecedat ut dispositio causans.
english: Thesis XXVIII. They also acknowledge that repentance, or penitence, is the condition on which the forgiveness of sins, in which a sinner's justification consists, is offered in the Gospel. So the celebrated Maresius teaches that forgiveness of sins belongs to repentance 'conditionally, inasmuch as it is offered to us in the Gospel on the condition of repentance and faith' (disputation On repentance and Christian liberty, thesis 32).

Likewise Ames, in Bellarmine Disarmed, book 5, on justifying faith, chapter 3, grants that penitence precedes justification as a disposition prerequisite in order, but not as a cause. The same can be seen in Chemnitz himself at the place just cited.

Yet penitence and repentance involve many good works, such as the resolve to live a new life, hatred of sin, and even some love of God, which arises from the hope of obtaining pardon from him. So a good number of good works precede justification. Indeed Ames, at the place already cited, expressly acknowledges that 'some love of God comes before the forgiveness of sins, or justification, as a prerequisite disposition', though 'no love precedes forgiveness as a causing disposition'.

source_text: XXIX. Unde est quod Davenantius asserere non formidat, Bona quaedam opera necessaria esse ad justificationem, ut conditiones concurrentes, vel praecursorias, licet non sint necessaria ut causae efficientes, aut meritoriae: in hisce vero bonis operibus numerat interna illa quae apud Deum magni momenti sunt, quamvis in oculos hominum non incurrant; ut dolere de peccato, detestari peccatum, humiliter se Deo subjicere, ad Dei misericordiam confugere, in Christo Mediatore spem figere, novae vitae propositum inire, aliaque consimilia. Divina enim misericordia non justificat, inquit, stipites, hoc est nihil agentes: neque equos & mulos, hoc est, recalcitrantes & libidinibus suis obstinate adhaerescentes: sed homines eosdemque compunctos & contritos, ac verbi spiritusque divini ductum sequentes. De justitia actuali cap. 31.
english: Thesis XXIX. Hence Davenant does not hesitate to assert that certain good works are necessary for justification as concurrent or preparatory conditions, though not as efficient or meritorious causes. Among these good works he counts inward ones that weigh much with God though men do not see them: grieving for sin, hating sin, humbly submitting to God, fleeing to God's mercy, setting one's hope on Christ the Mediator, resolving on a new life, and the like.

'For God's mercy,' he says, 'does not justify blocks of wood, that is, people who do nothing, nor horses and mules, that is, people who kick back and cling stubbornly to their lusts. It justifies men, and men who are pierced and contrite and follow the guidance of God's word and Spirit' (On actual righteousness, chapter 31).

source_text: XXX. Quod si bona quaedam opera praecedunt hominis justificationem, regenerationem ejus praecedere quoque debent: si quidem, ex communi Protestantium doctrina, regeneratio est justificatione natura posterior. Adde quod hominis regeneratio & sanctificatio reapse sunt unum & idem. Ac proinde spiritus quo homo regeneratur non est alius ab eo quo homo sanctificatur. Spiritus autem sanctificationis, ut expresse docent qui sunt inter Protestantes doctissimi atque celeberrimi, in Evangelio nobis non promittitur, nisi sub conditione fidei ejusque vivae atque efficacis, quae sine multis bonis operibus constare non potest. Nec datur ille spiritus, nisi iis qui serio cupientes ex vitiis emergere, & veram justitiam sitientes & esurientes, illum assiduis precibus ex fide factis a Deo postulant. Juxta illud Domini Jesu, Quanto magis Pater vester coelestis dabit spiritum sanctum petentibus ab ipso? Luc. 11. 13. Jam autem Deum ex fide orare proculdubio opus vere bonum est.
english: Thesis XXX. If some good works precede a man's justification, they must also precede his regeneration, since by the common doctrine of the Protestants regeneration comes after justification in the order of nature. Besides, a man's regeneration and his sanctification are in fact one and the same, so the Spirit by whom a man is regenerated is the same as the one by whom he is sanctified.

But the Spirit of sanctification, as the most learned and celebrated Protestants expressly teach, is promised to us in the Gospel only on the condition of faith, a living and effective faith, which cannot exist without many good works. Nor is that Spirit given except to those who earnestly want to rise out of their vices, who hunger and thirst for true righteousness, and who ask God for him in constant prayers made in faith.
As the Lord Jesus says, 'How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?' (Luke 11:13). And to pray to God in faith is certainly a truly good work.

source_text: XXXI. Atque huc etiam facit quod inter Protestantes viri magni nominis agnoscunt esse quasdam dispositiones ad sanctificationem, quae vi spiritus Dei excitantur in hominibus sanctificandis & regenerandis; quales sunt actus varii, fidei, timoris, dilectionis, ut videre est apud Paraeum in librum 1. Bellarmini de Justificatione cap. 3. Actus autem fidei atque dilectionis non possunt non esse bona quaedam opera; quae cum supponantur esse dispositiones quaedam ad sanctificationem, sive regenerationem, non possunt etiam non illam quodammodo antecedere.
english: Thesis XXXI. To the same point is the fact that Protestants of great name acknowledge certain dispositions to sanctification, aroused by the power of God's Spirit in people who are to be sanctified and regenerated. These are various acts of faith, fear and love, as can be seen in Pareus on Bellarmine's On justification, book 1, chapter 3.
Acts of faith and love cannot fail to be good works. And since they are taken to be dispositions to sanctification, or regeneration, they cannot fail to come before it in some way as well.

source_text: XXXII. Si ergo bona opera nonnulla, ex ipsa Protestantium Doctrina & confessione, antecedunt hominis regenerationem & justificationem, quomodo statuere possunt gratiam ipsam qua regeneramur atque justificamur necessariam esse ad quodvis opus bonum, & damnare canonem Concilii Tridentini, quo anathema pronunciatur in eos qui dicunt opera omnia quae ante justificationem fiunt, quacunque ratione facta sint, vere esse peccata?
english: Thesis XXXII. So if, by the Protestants' own doctrine and admission, some good works precede a man's regeneration and justification, how can they hold that the very grace by which we are regenerated and justified is necessary for every good work?
And how can they condemn the canon of the Council of Trent that pronounces anathema on those who say that all works done before justification, in whatever way they are done, are truly sins?
